events.event_narrative: Thunderstorm winds tossed an empty grain bin, and resulted in considerable tree damage. Minor roof damage was also done to the residence at this location. Property damage costs are a rough estimate.
Thunderstorm winds dented large grain bins on the southeast facing side, and numerous shingles were removed from the south side of a house. Property damage costs are a rough estimate.
Thunderstorm winds removed numerous shingles from a house. Property damage costs are a rough estimate.

A public video revealed that a tornado briefly spun up in an open field southwest of Salix between Benton Avenue and Interstate 29 north of 290th Street. The tornado traveled north northeast and lifted just south of 280th Street. The average path width was estimated at 20 yards.

This tornado formed around 4 miles east-northeast of Moville in Woodbury County and entered Plymouth County around two miles south of Kingsley, just east of the intersection of Knox Avenue and 100th Street.  Numerous large trees were snapped as the tornado entered Plymouth County. The tornado continued to travel north-northeast to a location around one mile east of Kingsley where several outbuildings were destroyed and large trees snapped.  The tornado then turned to a northerly track as it crossed County Road C66, where it damaged several power poles.  The tornado traveled another mile and a half parallel to Roosevelt Avenue before it destroyed a hoop barn and removed the steel roof from a corn crib, with debris scattered a half mile to the north.  The tornado dissipated after another quarter mile at 1642CST. The tornado was rated EF1 while in both Woodbury and Plymouth Counties. The average path width in Plymouth County was 50 yards and the maximum estimated wind speed was 105 mph. Property damage costs are a rough estimate.

This tornado formed around 4 miles east-northeast of Moville, one-quarter mile east of the intersection of Jasper Avenue and 140th Street. The tornado traveled north-northeast for slightly over 4 and one quarter miles before exiting Woodbury County two miles south of Kingsley, just east of the intersection of Knox Avenue and 100th Street.  The tornado continued in Plymouth County for somewhat less than 4 miles before dissipating at 1642CST.  In Woodbury County near the touchdown point, a barn roof was collapsed.  The tornado continued northeast for around a mile and a half before removing most roof panels from another barn. Near the Plymouth County line, the tornado encountered another farmstead which suffered total destruction of a garage and outbuilding. Numerous larger trees were snapped, and debris from damaged buildings was deposited in the trees. The tornado was rated EF1 while in both Woodbury and Plymouth Counties. The average path width in Woodbury County was 50 yards and the maximum estimated wind speed was 110 mph. Property damage costs are a rough estimate.
An old barn was pushed off its foundation and partially collapsed.

A tornado formed in an open field between 280th and 290th Streets near the Woodbury and Ida County line southwest of Battle Creek.  The tornado tracked northeast for around one mile before it removed shingles from a house southwest of Battle Creek. As the tornado continued northeast, four additional farmsteads were impacted with|several outbuildings damaged or destroyed. Several trees were damaged and a few power poles were snapped north of Battle Creek. The tornado crossed U.S. Highway 59 just north of 190th Street, and lifted approximately 7 miles north of Ida Grove. The average path width was 50 yards and the maximum estimated wind speed was 100 mph. Property damage costs are a rough estimate.

Thunderstorm winds caused the collapse of a brick gable on the west side of a building at the Grand Meadow Heritage Center, as well as lesser damage to other buildings. Property damage costs are a rough estimate.

Thunderstorms winds removed a portion of the roof of a well-built machine shed. Property damage costs are a rough estimate.

This tornado formed on the southeast fringes of Larrabee, just south of 455th Street. As the tornado crossed 455th Street, it quickly destroyed four silos, a shed and a chicken barn. The tornado traveled northeast over open fields before a few trees were snapped and the east wall of a barn was pulled away along R Avenue just south of 430th Street.  The tornado exited Cherokee County around 4 miles south of Sutherland, one-half mile east of the intersection of Tyler Avenue and 420th Street. The tornado continued in O'Brien County for almost 4 miles before dissipating two miles southeast of Sutherland at 1711CST. The tornado was rated EF1 while in both Cherokee County and O'Brien County. The average path width in Cherokee County was 50 yards and the maximum estimated wind speed was 105 mph. Property damage costs are a rough estimate.

This tornado formed on the southeast edge of Larrabee in Cherokee County, just south of 455th Street. The tornado entered O'Brien County around 4 miles south of Sutherland, one-half mile east of the intersection of Tyler Avenue and 420th Street. The tornado continued northeast in O'Brien County for almost 4 miles, and resulted in only sporadic tree damage before destroying a shed and scattered debris across State Highway 10 two miles south-southeast of Sutherland. The tornado tore part of a roof off a shed shortly before it dissipated two miles southeast of Sutherland at 1711CST. The tornado was rated EF1 while in both Cherokee County and O'Brien County. The average path width in O'Brien County was 75 yards and the maximum estimated wind speed was 105 mph. Property damage costs are a rough estimate.
Thunderstorm winds snapped several large trees and limbs, which fell and destroyed the roof of a machine shed. Property damage costs are a rough estimate.
Thunderstorm winds downed severe large diameter tree limbs.

The tornado developed 2 miles north-northwest of Galva, one-half mile southwest of the intersection of 120th Street and Landmark Avenue.  The tornado tracked northeast to a farmstead on the northeast corner of the intersection, where a hoop barn was destroyed and the roof partially removed from a residence. The tornado exited Ida County 4 miles north of Galva just east of Marshal Avenue at 1700CST. The tornado clipped the far southeast corner of Cherokee County, then entered Buena Vista County at 1701CST, where the tornado lifted one mile southwest of Alta at 1706CST. The tornado was rated EF0 in Ida County, EFU in Cherokee County, and EF1 in Buena Vista County. The average path width in Ida County was 50 yards and the maximum estimated wind speed was 85 mph. Property damage costs are a rough estimate.

This is the second segment of a tornado which developed 2 miles north-northwest of Galva at 1658CST, and entered Cherokee County 4 miles north of Galva just east of Marshal Avenue at 1700CST. The tornado tracked over open farmland in extreme southeast Cherokee County with no damage indicators, before it entered Buena Vista County at 1701CST, where the tornado lifted one mile southwest of Alta at 1706CST. The tornado was rated EF0 in Ida County, EFU in Cherokee County, and EF1 in Buena Vista County. The average path width in Cherokee County was estimated at 50 yards.

This is the third segment of a tornado which developed 2 miles north-northwest of Galva at 1658CST, and tracked northeast through extreme southeast Cherokee County. The tornado entered Buena Vista County at 1701CST, one-half mile south of the intersection of 10th Avenue and 640th Street. Along 640th Street, the tornado destroyed two outbuildings on a farmstead and damaged three others, removed a chimney from the roof of the residence, downed several light poles, and snapped and uprooted several large trees. Numerous other large trees were snapped or uprooted as the tornado tracked northeast over the next two miles, before damaging the roof of a hog confinement along 620th Street between 20th and 30th Avenues. Several houses lost shingles and siding, with occasional tree damage before the tornado lifted one mile southwest of Alta at 1706CST. The tornado was rated EF0 in Ida County, EFU in Cherokee County, and EF1 in Buena Vista County. The average path width in Buena Vista County was 50 yards and the maximum estimated wind speed was 100 mph. Property damage costs are a rough estimate.
Several large branches were downed by thunderstorm winds.

The tornado spun up just north of Rembrandt at 1718CST near the intersection of 120th Avenue and 470th Street. The tornado tracked northeast, and dissipated near the Little Sioux River one mile east of Sioux Rapids at 1722CST.  A residence near the touchdown had siding and roofing torn from the home, along with snapped large pine trees. Along 460th Street just west of U.S. Highway 71, several large wooden power poles were snapped.  The tornado continued northeast, crossing U.S. 71 one-half mile north of 460th Street where it destroyed several small buildings.  More power poles were snapped along 450th Street east of U.S. 71, with the final damage noted in snapped trees along the Little Sioux River east of Sioux Rapids.  The average path width was 75 yards and the maximum estimated wind speed was 115 mph. Property damage costs are a rough estimate.

The tornado spun up 7 miles south-southwest of Aurelia just west of the intersection of T Avenue and 610th Street. The tornado moved either northeast or north-northeast along its track and exited Cherokee County at 1707CST near the intersection of 510th Street and 10th Avenue. The tornado continued northeast and lifted one mile south of the Buena Vista County Conservation Park at 1712CST.  ||Shortly after touchdown, the tornado partially collapsed the roof on a hog confinement which killed 13 hogs. Debris from this building was strewn for one to two miles to the northeast.  On a northeastward track, another animal confinement farm was struck by the tornado after a couple minutes which resulted in loss of several roof panels on multiple buildings. At this point the tornado shifted path toward more of a north-northeast direction and moved into Aurelia.  A drying unit was removed from the top of a grain elevator on the south edge of town.  Most of the damage throughout the eastern half of Aurelia was snapped trees, which caused collateral damage to numerous roofs and windows along the path. The tornado moved through the golf course snapping and uprooting numerous trees. The tornado continued with a shift to a more northeast track, and destroyed a barn and three outbuildings along 535th Street northeast of Aurelia. Additional damage occurred to a machine shed and large trees along the Cherokee and Buena Vista County line. The tornado was rated EF1 in both Cherokee and Buena Vista Counties. The average path width was 150 yards in Cherokee County and the maximum estimated wind speed was 110 mph. Property damage costs are a rough estimate.

The tornado which spun up 7 miles south-southwest of Aurelia continued into Buena Vista County at 1707CST near the intersection of 510th Street and 10th Avenue. The tornado continued northeast and lifted one mile south of the Buena Vista County Conservation Park at 1712CST.  Along the track, the tornado caused siding and roof damage to outbuildings near 20th Ave and 490th Street, and removed walls of a machine shed along 480th Street west of 30th Avenue. Numerous wooden power poles were snapped along 470th and 460th Streets. The tornado was rated EF1 in both Cherokee and Buena Vista Counties. The average path width was 75 yards in Buena Vista County and the maximum estimated wind speed was 110 mph. Property damage costs are a rough estimate.

A tornado spun up 3 miles east-northeast of Fostoria one-half mile south of 260th Street east of 250th Avenue.  The tornado tracked north just east of 250th Avenue, and snapped several power poles along 260th and 250th Streets.  Two farms between 250th and 240th Streets were struck by the tornado, which peeled back the roof of an outbuilding and damaged several large trees.  The most significant damage occurred along 235th Street where a portion of the south-facing roof was removed from a house and an outbuilding to the north of the house was destroyed.  The tornado tracked through open fields for another mile before it lifted 2 miles east of Milford. The average path width was 25 yards and the maximum estimated wind speed was 100 mph. Property damage costs are a rough estimate.

A pole barn was destroyed by strong wind gusts on the edge of Chamberlain.

A fire broke out midday along U.S. Highway 20 between Ponca and Willis, and quickly spread to over 190 acres. The fire consumed more than 40 hay bales at one farm. One firefighter was injured and taken to the hospital, but released later in the evening.

To the northeast of Adrian, strong winds caused a powerline leading into a barn to arc, and sparks ignited material stored in the hayloft.  The fire totally consumed the barn and two other outbuildings, and killed 17 sheep housed in the barn.  The fire then raced to the northeast a quarter mile into an adjoining property and burned grassland and numerous hay bales.  A second fire started in a burn pit near the Lismore dump when embers from a previous days burn reignited, but was quickly contained.
A wildfire consumed around 200 acres of grassland and light timber. One tractor was a complete loss when it burned attempting to plow a fire line.

Three area fire departments responded to a fire around 3 miles north-northwest of Lesterville, sparked by an electrical cord hanging from a silage unloader.  A 30 by 30 foot shed and a large grove of trees were burned.

A grassfire erupted 3 miles southeast of Merrill near the intersection of Key Avenue and 250th Street, and spread rapidly to the northeast.  The wind-driven fire scorched more than 1000 acres, destroying one home on the southwest corner of the intersection of County Road C44 and Lake Avenue.  At one point, seven area fire departments were on the fire.  This was the most significant of five concurrent fires across the county.  Visibility was near zero at times with smoke and blowing dust, and this resulted in one firefighting vehicle getting stuck in a ditch, overtaken and burned by the rapidly moving fire.

A tornado spun up just west of 280th Avenue around one-half mile south of 51st Street, where several tree limbs were broken in a tree line. The tornado tracked northeast across the Des Moines River where more limbs were downed into the river near 290th Avenue.  As the tornado took a slightly more north-northeast turn for about one-third mile, the most significant damage occurred at a farmstead where one silo was toppled and another damaged, along with numerous downed tree limbs.  The tornado continued more northeastward for around one mile where it damaged the north end of a barn and spread debris around one-quarter mile to the northeast into Cottonwood County. The tornado continued in Cottonwood County for less than one-third mile before dissipating at 1637CST. The tornado was rated EF1 while in Murray County, and EFU in Cottonwood County. The estimated maximum wind speed was 90 mph and the average path width in Murray County was 50 yards.

This tornado formed 5 miles east-northeast of Fulda in Murray County, and entered Cottonwood County around 6 miles south-southwest of Westbrook. The tornado tracked northeast over open fields for less than a minute before dissipating.  While in Murray County, it was rated EF1, but was rated EFU in Cottonwood County. Average path width in Cottonwood County was 50 yards.

A tornado spun up around one mile west-southwest of Storden just southeast of the intersection of State Highway 30 and 370th Avenue.  The tornado tracked northeast and crossed a slough where grasses exhibited a convergent pattern. The tornado then moved into the northwest edge of Storden where it destroyed a 500,000 bushel commercial grain bin and tossed the debris onto an adjacent office structure.  The tornado lifted before reaching County Road 5. The estimated maximum wind speed was 95 mph and the average path width was 50 yards.

A tornado spun up just north of the intersection of 41st Street and Western Avenue, where it uprooted a large tree. The tornado travelled generally eastward for around one-half mile before it dissipated one block south of the Augustana University athletic fields. Two garage structures collapsed along the track, with some roof damage to adjacent homes. Numerous trees were topped or uprooted, with one tree falling on an unoccupied car. The estimated maximum wind speed was 95 mph and the average path width was 50 yards.

A tornado developed approximately two miles east of Brandon, just south of State Highway 138 west of 484th Avenue.  The tornado moved eastward and toppled several large trees shortly after touchdown, then turned to more of a east-southeast direction. After tracking about one-quarter mile, the tornado did the greatest damage along its track at the Beaver Valley Lutheran Church, where a large portion of the roof was removed.  The tornado continued another couple tenths of a mile across open fields before it dissipated. The estimated maximum wind speed was 105 mph and the average path width was 50 yards.

A tornado spun up near the intersection of Fig Avenue and 140th Street.  On a northeastward track, the tornado impacted two farmsteads around a mile apart, with significant roof damage done to outbuildings at each location, as well as destruction of a  large grain bin.  The tornado tracked a few hundred yards beyond the final farm before dissipating in an open field. The estimated maximum wind was 90 mph and the average path width was 75 yards.

A brief tornado developed on the south side of Doon, and traveled northeast across the southeast side of town before it dissipated at the eastern edge of town. The estimated maximum wind was 85 mph and the average path width was 50 yards.

A historic snowfall pummeled the area with two distinct periods of heavy snowfall, which totaled as much as 18 to 27 inches in the northern portion of the county, including 26.5 inches 4 miles west-northwest of Dell Rapids, 25.5 inches at Humboldt, and 23.3 inches 4 miles north-northwest of Renner. Snow fell at a rate of 2 to 3 inches per hour at times during the afternoon of January 2 and the morning of January 3. Schools and government offices were closed, and the Sioux Falls Airport ceased operations for almost 24 hours. Over 190 vehicles were stranded on Sioux Falls city streets, along with 27 non-injury accidents and 3 indirect injury accidents.

A landspout quickly spun up around 2 miles northwest of Windom in an open field just north of the Windom Country Club.  The weak tornado moved just east of north and crossed 405th Street, where it glanced a farmstead and caused damage to shingles on an outbuilding. The tornado continued about a half mile across open fields before turning more northerly, and crossed 395th Street before lifting less than a quarter mile farther to the north. The maximum wind speed was 65 mph and the average path width was 20 yards.

A tornado spun up just north of the Sac-Buena Vista County border between 90th and 100th Avenue. The circulation featured intermittent contact with the surface for the next mile, as the tornado tracked a bit more westward after crossing 90th Avenue. There were no damage indicators impacted along the track, which was documented fully on storm chaser video. An EF rating could not be determined and the average path width was estimated to be 50 yards.

A tornado quickly spun up east of 230th Avenue and north of 620th Street in an open field. The tornado traveled to the north-northwest for several minutes, then crossed roadways near the intersection of 230th Avenue and 600th Street.  The tornado impacted a small farmstead on the west side of 230th Avenue where it tore several shingles off an old barn and damaged numerous branches and several rotted trees. The tornado continued another quarter mile to the northwest before lifting. The maximum wind speed was 75 mph and the average path width was 50 yards.

A tornado spun up quickly at 1504 CST beneath a rapidly intensifying storm just north of 302nd Street in an open field between 425th and 426th Avenue. The tornado crawled through open country toward the north-northwest for several minutes and crossed Beaver Creek before damaging several trees on a farmstead along 425th Avenue. The tornado also ripped tin off an abandoned outbuilding. At this point, the tornado track veered to the north as it moved through soybean fields and across 301st Street before it lifted around a tenth of a mile north of 301st Street. The average path width for the tornado was 30 yards. The tornado was rated an EF-0 with a maximum estimated wind gust of 74 mph.

A no travel advised order was put out with numerous roads under significant flowing water up to mid-vehicle depth, including 2nd Avenue SE near New Age Church and 4th Avenue SE near Children's Park. Property damage costs are rough estimates.

Water ponding in the area of Central Park overflowed roadways and entered the Sioux Center Fire Department building. Two homes suffered the collapse of basement walls from the high water. Water also inundated a transformer which cut off power to seven homes in the northwest part of town. Seven trailers were evacuated due to high water in Westbrook Village on the northwest edge of town. More than two dozen vehicles were stranded in high water. Damage costs are rough estimates.

A highly visible tornado developed a quarter mile south of Iowa Highway 10 just to the east of Goldfinch Avenue. The slow-moving tornado was photographed by several members of the public as it tracked generally a bit south of due eastward.  Very soon after touching down, the tornado impacted a shelter belt where it did damage to several hardwood trees.  After a quarter mile, the tornado track shifted slightly toward the east-northeast across open farmland. The tornado crossed Grant Avenue and lifted shortly thereafter.  The average path width was 25 yards. The tornado was rated an EF-0 with a maximum wind speed of 75 mph.
A thunderstorm wind gust to 71 mph was measured by a law enforcement officer.  Some minor damage to shingles and trees was observed near the point the wind was measured.

A very old barn collapsed under the weight of a more modern roof. The structure fell to the southeast, most likely in relation to rear flank downdraft wind on the backside of tornado producing mesocyclone. Property damage costs are a rough estimate.

A report was relayed through De Smet Fire of a brief tornado which touched down north of 201st Street just south of Mud Lake.  The tornado tracked eastward across open grass and marsh lands for around one-half mile before reaching the southern portion of Mud Lake where the tornado was observed pulling up water shortly before dissipating.  The average path width was 20 yards. The tornado did not cause any damage to allow designation of a rating.

A tornado spun up initially around one-third mile southeast of the intersection of 202nd Street and 442nd Aveune. A video documented the tornado as it tracked east-northeast across open fields for around one mile before lifting just south of 202nd Street approximately one-half mile east of 443rd Avenue.  The tornado caused no known damage to incur a rating. The average path width was 20 yards.

A tornado touched down around 1 mile west-southwest of Kinbrae, just south of 120th Street to the east of Town Avenue.  The tornado traveled northeast and crossed the road, where the tornado passed through a farmstead and removed a few metal panels from a farm outbuilding. After the tornado left a path across a corn field while it moved another one-half mile northeast, the tornado impacted a tree line and uprooted a large pine tree.  The tornado continued across open fields with a slightly more eastward turn, then lifted near the intersection of 110th Street and Ulrich Avenue.  The path was captured by a local resident with a drone, with an average path width of 40 yards. The tornado was rated an EF-0 with a maximum wind speed of 80 mph. Property damage costs are a rough estimate.

A storm chaser witnessed a very brief touchdown in an open soybean field between 470th and 471st Avenue and 199th and 200th Street. The lack of damage indicators did not allow for a rating of this tornado.

Multiple storm chasers reported development of swirling debris at the surface below a funnel cloud north of 205th Street and east of 468th Avenue around 3 miles east-southeast of Bruce.  Debris was witnessed near the surface as the slow-moving tornado tracked for a few minutes northeast through an open field. The tornado lifted just south of 204th Street.  The average path width was estimated at 15 yards with a maximum width of 20 yards. However, the lack of damage indicators did not allow for a rating of this tornado.

Multiple storm chasers witnessed a tornado develop in an open field south of 202nd Street and west of 470th Avenue.  The tornado tracked very slowly north-northeast with the track defined by field debris circulating near the surface. The tornado lifted just west of 470th Avenue around one-half mile north of 202nd Street. The average path width was estimated at 15 yards with a maximum width of 20 yards. However, the lack of damage indicators did not allow for a rating of this tornado.

A storm chaser witnessed a very brief tornado along 479th Avenue just south of the intersection with 197th Street, around 6 miles north of White. The touchdown was evident by swirling field debris, but no damage indicator was present to allow for a rating of the tornado.

A spin up developed around one-half mile north-northeast of Leota. A storm chaser witnessed field debris lofted and circulated by the very brief funnel just west of Birkett Avenue. There were no damage indicators present to allow for a rating of this tornado.

In nearby rural areas, numerous fields were flooded, causing an unknown amount of crop damage. Small streams such as Pony Creek in Parkston flooded, adding to the damage.

A tornado spun up in an open field around 4 miles southwest of Struble, about one-half mile south of 130th Street and just west of Kestrel Avenue.  The tornado tracked to the northeast for one-half mile before destroying an outbuilding and blowing out a garage door on a single family dwelling on the east side of Kestrel Avenue.  The tornado continued northeast for around one mile before it uprooted a one-foot diameter tree at another farmstead before it lifted shortly thereafter. The maximum estimated wind speed was 105 mph and the average path width was 25 yards.

A brief tornado spun up just south of 380th Street on the outskirts of Sioux Center. The tornado quickly crossed 380th Street as it moved north-northeast and uprooted several large pine trees along a tree line. The tornado then struck a farmstead where it collapsed a barn and tossed tin into a neighboring field. The tornado shifted track to a more northeast direction and then crossed open fields until it lifted near the railroad tracks around one-half mile south of 370th Street. The maximum estimated wind speed was 85 mph and the average path width was 25 yards.

The tornado moved northeast for about another minute before breaking several large branches at a residence before it lifted. The maximum estimated wind speed was 80 mph and the average path width was 25 yards.

A tornado developed along 270th Street to the west of Kennedy Avenue. It tracked north-northeastward through Otter Valley Golf Course where it uprooted several trees and damaged a maintenance shed. The tornado continued on a north-northeast path and impacted a farmstead north of the golf course where it destroyed an outbuilding and uprooted several more trees. Debris from the outbuilding was strewn across a field as it continued for another half mile northward before it lifted near the intersection of 260th Street and Kennedy Avenue. The maximum estimated wind speed was 105 mph and the average path width was 50 yards.

A tornado spun up just south of IA Highway 3 and west of 70th Avenue. The tornado tracked north-northeast for around 0.2 mile before removing roof panels from an outbuilding and tearing several limbs off a large tree. The tornado crossed Highway 3 where it snapped the tops from several hardwood trees. The tornado tracked for another half mile across open fields before impacting a farmstead where it removed the roof from an older residence and mangled several trees. The attached garage was shifted 6 to 10 inches off its foundation. The tornado then took a slightly more northeastward track over the next half mile, crossed 520th Street to another farm where it blew doors out of a garage, damaged empty grain bins and broke numerous tree limbs. The tornado lifted after another 0.3 mile across an open field. The estimated peak wind was 110 mph and the average path width was 50 yards.

A tornado formed on the far eastern edge of Sheldon near the Crossroads Pavilion. The tornado tracked north-northwest for around one-quarter mile and crossed U.S. Highway 18 at the intersection of 34th Avenue. North of Highway 18, the tornado impacted an RV dealership where the roof was partially peeled off a machine shed and several RVs were flipped or destroyed. Several roof panels of two other buildings were also peeled off. Debris was strewn across an open field to the northwest over the next one-third mile before the tornado crossed Nest Avenue shortly before it lifted. The maximum estimated wind speed was 85 mph and the average path width was 50 yards.

Rainfall amounts across Union County from June 20-22 ranged from around a third of an inch across southern areas to 1 to 2 inches across northern areas. At the peak of the flooding, there were an estimated 20 to 30 water rescues.  ||Residents along Northshore and Penrose Drives on the north side of McCook Lake were evacuated on the evening of June 23 as flood waters rose rapidly. On January 26, a young girl was crossing South Dakota Highway 34 about 10 miles west of Wessington Springs to board a school bus when she was struck by a vehicle. The vehicle engaged its breaks when flashing lights on the bus became more visible in dense fog and then slid on the icy road, hitting the young girl. The girl sustained serious, life-threatening injuries and succumbed to those injuries (indirect fatality) on February 6.

Thunderstorm winds caused widespread damage in and near Sioux City. Tree damage included large trees blown down, blocking several roads. A few vehicles were destroyed and numerous vehicles damaged by falling trees and tree debris. Falling trees also damaged several residences and garages, causing one known injury. The winds lifted a three car garage off its foundation, and overturned it onto a nearby pasture. One large tree split an occupied trailer in the middle, missing residents who were sleeping at both ends. Numerous power lines and poles were blown down or broken, leaving an estimated 19,000 customers without power, several thousand of which were still without power 24 hours later. Numerous buildings, especially residences, sustained roof damage, especially to shingles. The winds damaged or blew down several signs, damaged fences, and blew down a large awning that sheltered gasoline pumps at a convenience store. The winds flattened crops near the city, but the amount of crop damage was not known, especially since crops were expected to partially recover.

A storm chaser documented the initial touchdown of a tornado a little over a mile to the northwest of Dixon, SD just north of 276th Street in an open field. The tornado traveled to the east-southeast for around 2 miles before it impacted the north side of a farmstead where it damaged the shelter belt and destroyed an older outbuilding. As it continued along the path, it crossed near the intersection of SD 47 and SD 44 where it downed power poles and twisted a couple of SDDOT truck shelters. The tornado then traveled over mainly open fields for another 2 to 3 miles before taking a slight turn more to the southeast. After around 5 more miles on a southeastward path, the tornado lifted in an area of more uneven terrain. The tornado was rated EF1 with an estimated maximum wind gust of 110 mph. The average path width was around 100 yards.
A funnel cloud developed over White Lake.

A storm chaser documented the initial touchdown of a tornado less than one mile northwest of Lucas, SD a bit southeast of the intersection of 283rd Street and 347th Avenue. The tornado then tracked southeast for around one mile, narrowly missing the town of Lucas but uprooting three large pine trees at 284th Street and 348th Avenue. After crossing the intersection, the tornado shredded the tree line just to the east of a hunting lodge. The tornado traveled across an open section before turning more southerly and again impacting a tree line at the mid-section line. The tornado crossed 349th Avenue and left a track in some mature corn before lifting just east of 349th Avenue. The tornado was rated EF0 with an estimated maximum wind gust of 85 mph. The average path width was 25 yards.

This was the third tornado documented by a storm chaser across Gregory County. This tornado touched down west of Whetstone Bay on the Missouri River, north of Whetstone Township Highway and to the west of County Road 57.  After a very short distance, the tornado broke multiple power poles along County Road 57 as it traveled south-southeast. The tornado then traveled for 5 miles across unpopulated complex terrain with no road access, although its damage path was visible on Copernicus Sentinel data 2025. Coming out of the hills, the tornado hit a single family dwelling, with the collapse of all exterior walls among other major damage. Two nearby outbuildings were also destroyed. The tornado continued to the south-southeast for approximately 1.5 miles before it flipped a camper and destroyed an abandoned trailer on the north side of Bonesteel. The tornado lifted a few hundred yards north of Eldeen Avenue, missing the city-center of Bonesteel. The tornado was rated EF2 with an estimated maximum wind gust of 135 mph. The average path width was estimated at 125 yards.

A tornado spun up approximately 1 mile east-northeast of Alvord just north of 210th Street and around one-half mile west of Fig Avenue. The tornado traveled southeast one-half mile to Fig Avenue where it destroyed a small shed and heavily damaged an abandoned farmstead, including a grove of old trees. A distinct convergent path was noted in the corn just north of the farmstead. One mile farther east-southeast, the tornado destroyed a barn along Fir Avenue. After traveling another one-half mile through fields, the tornado lifted east of Fir Avenue. The tornado was rated EF1 with an estimated maximum wind gust of 110 mph. The average path width was 100 yards.

A wildfire ignited southeast of Bronson around 3:00 pm and rapidly spread northeastward. The wildfire ended just north of U.S. Highway 20 east of Lawton around 9:00 pm. The wildfire perimeter was approximately 7.1 miles long by 1.4 miles wide, burning 3400 acres. No fatalities were reported, but one injury occurred. Multiple pets and livestock were killed. Two single-family homes, 15 to 20 outbuildings, and one county bridge were destroyed.

A tornado developed a little less than one mile north of Webb just east of 290th Avenue in an open field.  The tornado was documented by numerous individuals as it tracked east-northeast for a little over a minute. The tornado crossed 300th Avenue near a farmstead where trees were damaged along the north side of the property and the resultant winds caused minor damage to the residence.  The tornado continued toward the east-northeast for a little over a minute over open fields and lifted just before 310th Avenue south of 470th Street. The tornado was rated EF0 with a maximum estimated wind speed of 75 mph. The average path width was 30 yards.
A personal weather station measured a wind gust to 72 mph with some damage to shingles and siding on a residence.  Wind-driven hail also knocked out windows on a camper.

After crossing Pierce Avenue, the tornado dissipated. There was no known damage, resulting in an EFU rating. The location, track, and a maximum path width of 25 yards was estimated from video.

These winds combined with the heavy snowfall to produce widespread visibilities below a quarter mile from Christmas day to the start of the next day. Most roads were blocked and travel was brought to a standstill, as was the limited holiday commerce.

Rapid melting of a heavy winter snowpack caused flooding of the Big Sioux River which resulted in a record high stage near Bruce. Several fields and roads were flooded. The river crested at 3.2 feet above flood stage near Bruce on March 16th, and at 3.1 feet above flood stage near Brookings on March 9th.

Rapid melting of a heavy winter snowpack caused flooding of the Big Sioux River which resulted in minor to moderate flooding. Several fields and a few roads were flooded, as was the Flandreau city park. The river crested at 1.2 feet above flood stage at Flandreau on March 17th.

Rapid melting of a heavy winter snowpack caused flooding of the Big Sioux River which resulted in moderate flooding. Several fields and roads were flooded. Rapid melting of a heavy winter snowpack caused flooding of the Big Sioux River which resulted in major flooding along part of the river. Several fields and roads were flooded. The river crested at 7.5 feet above flood stage at Hawarden, Iowa on March 16th.

Rapid melting of a heavy winter snowpack caused flooding of the Big Sioux River which resulted in moderate to major flooding. Several fields and roads were flooded. The river crested at 6.4 feet above flood stage several miles northeast of Richland on March 17th. A damaged dike near this location caused more widespread flooding of cropland, and also resulted in the flooding and closing of South Dakota Highway 48 in the area.

Rapid melting of a heavy winter snowpack caused flooding of Skunk Creek and Willow Creek, with each cresting around 2 feet above flood stage near Hartford and Crooks. Fields along the creeks were flooded.

Rapid melting of a heavy winter snowpack caused flooding of the Big Sioux River which resulted in major flooding along part of the river. Several fields and roads were flooded. The snowmelt also caused the Rock River to flood. It crested at 4 feet above flood stage at Rock rapids on March 15th.

Rapid melting of a heavy winter snowpack caused flooding of the Big Sioux River which resulted in major flooding along part of the river. Several fields and roads were flooded. The river crested at 6.4 feet above flood stage at Akron on March 17th.

The Vermillion River crested at 3.6 feet above flood stage near Wakonda on March 14th, and 6.4 feet above flood stage near Vermillion on March 20th.

Rapid melting of a heavy winter snowpack resulted in major to record flooding of the Vermillion River, including the east and West Fork Vermillion Rivers. Fields and most county and smaller roads were flooded with some roads washed out. U.S. Highway 18 near Davis was flooded and closed. Homes and businesses were flooded, especially in the hard hit town of Davis, but also in and near Centerville, where ice jams and at least two broken dikes added to the flooding problems. The Vermillion River crested at 5.4 feet above flood stage near Davis on March 15th. The East and West Fork Vermillion Rivers crested at 2 and 3.2 feet above flood stage, respectively, near Parker on march 14th.

Rapid melting of a heavy winter snowpack resulted in moderate to major flooding of the Little Vermillion River. Numerous fields and roads were flooded with some roads washed out. The Little Vermillion River crested at 2.3 feet above flood stage near Salem on March 14th.

Rapid melting of a heavy winter snowpack resulted in moderate to major flooding of the Little Sioux River. Fields and other lowlands as well as roads near the river were flooded. The Little Sioux River crested at 4.65 feet above flood stage near Milford on March 17th.

Rapid melting of a heavy winter snowpack resulted in moderate to major flooding of the Little Sioux River. Fields and other lowlands as well as roads near the river were flooded. The Little Sioux River crested at 5.6 feet above flood stage at Spencer on March 16th.

Rapid melting of a heavy winter snowpack caused minor lowland flooding along the Rock River in Sioux County. The river crested at a half a foot above flood stage at Rock valley on March 15th.

A tornado, moving into Osceola County from Lyon County, destroyed at least two houses, injuring two people in one of them. the tornado also destroyed several garages and severely damaged several other homes, destroyed at least 4 hog confinement buildings, several barns and silos, and numerous outbuildings. The tornado destroyed three vehicles that had been parked under an Iowa Highway 60 overpass, injuring 11 people in the vehicles, and removing the engine from one of the vehicles. The tornado damaged power lines, causing power outages, and caused damage to trees and crops. The tornado also destroyed a shelter belt and severely damaged heavy farm equipment, removing the wheels from some of the vehicles. Moderate to major flooding of the James River was observed for most of the month. The river, which has been slowly falling before June, rose again due to heavy rain, and the number of fields and roads flooded increased again. Several roads in Huron were closed, and a swimming pool was closed due to the river flooding the parking lot. The river crested at near 5.7 feet above flood stage at Huron, or about 3 feet below the March crest.

Moderate to major flooding of the James River was observed for most of the month. The river, which has been slowly falling before June, rose again due to heavy rain, and the number of fields and roads flooded increased again. The river crested at near 6.5 feet above flood stage at Forestburg, which was a little more then half a foot below the March crest.

Recurring heavy rainfall caused major flooding of Firesteel Creek from early June to just before the end of the month. The creek crested at 7.3 feet above flood stage near Mount Vernon on June 13th, or about three quarters of a foot below the record March crest.

Recurring heavy rain cause moderate to major flooding of the Big Sioux River. Several roads and fields along the river were flooded. The river crested at just over 3 feet above flood stage near Bruce on June 14th, and also a little over 3 feet above flood stage near Brookings on June 17th. The flooding abated late in the month, but increased again starting on June 27th as more heavy rain fell.

Recurring heavy rain cause minor to moderate flooding of the Big Sioux River. Some l roads and fields along the river were flooded. While the river remained a little below flood stage at Flandreau, flooding occured both north and south of that point, with the moderate flooding near the northern edge of the county. The flooding abated late in the month, but minor flooding developed again after June 27th as more heavy rain fell.

Recurring heavy rain cause minor flooding of the Big Sioux River. A few lowland areas along the river sustained minor flooding. The river crested at less than a foot over flood stage at Dell Rapids and Sioux Falls.

Recurring heavy rain cause moderate flooding of the Big Sioux River. Some  roads and fields along the river were flooded. The river crested at just under 4 feet above flood stage near Hawarden, Iowa on June 30th.

Recurring heavy rain cause moderate flooding of the Big Sioux River. Some  roads and fields along the river were flooded. The river crested at just over 3 feet above flood stage near Akron, Iowa, or several miles northeast of Richland, South Dakota, on June 23rd.
Recurring heavy rain cause minor flooding of Skunk and Willow Creeks, with each cresting at less than a foot above flood stage. A few small lowland areas sustained minor flooding.

Repeating heavy rain caused minor to moderate flooding of the Floyd River. Some lowlands including farmland along the river were affected. The river crested at 2.26 feet aboce flood stage at Alton on June 23rd.

Heavy rain caused minor to moderate flooding of the Vermillion River, including the East and West fork Vermillion Rivers. Lowlands, fields, and some roads were flooded. The Vermillion River crested at 3.6 feet above flood stage near Davis on June 15th. The East Fork Vermillion River crested at 1 feet above flood stage on June 15th, and the west Fork crested at a little more than 2 feet above flood stage on June 11th, both near Parker.

Heavy rain caused moderate to record flooding along the Little Sioux River, with lowlands including land and several roads near the river flooded. Several roads were flooded on the south side of the town of Cherokee, including U.S. Highway 59 which was under much water, the state Highway 3 bypass, and several other roads. Up to 200 people were evacuated from the south side of Cherokee, where several businesses were flooded, and where access was cut off to areas not flooded. The river rose very rapidly and crested at a record 10.3 feet above flood stage at Cherokee on June 27th, which was the day after the flooding began.

Melting of a heavy winter snow cover caused major flooding of the James River, as well as flooding of small streams and lakes in the county. Farmland was also flooded, both near to and away from the James River. The James River crested at 9.16 feet above flood stage at Huron on March 26th. Over 50 miles of roads were closed by the flooding, including South Dakota Highway 28 in the eastern part of the county. Water was running over other roads, from flooded streams, creeks, and fields as well as from the James River. The flooding onset was rapid for a snow melt flood due to high water and groundwater levels from record precipitation in the year 2010.

Major flooding of the James River, as well as flooding of small streams and lakes in the county, continued through April. Much farmland remained flooded, both near to and away from the James River. The James River was 7.3 feet above flood stage at Huron on April 1st, and fell very slowly during the month. Over 50 miles of roads remained closed by the flooding at the start of the month, including South Dakota Highway 28 in the eastern part of the county. Water was running over other roads, from flooded streams, creeks, and fields as well as from the James River. Many roads were heavily damaged. The damage to township and county roads alone was estimated near the end of April at 1.7 million dollars. Some homes and businesses were also flooded, with the flooding of these places slowly alleviating through the month. High water and groundwater levels from record precipitation in the year 2010, a main reason the flooding onset was so fast in March, was also a main reason that the flooding subsided so slowly during April.

A large camper in the city park was overturned. The winds and tree debris also damaged power lines, causing a power outage. Tree debris blocked numerous roads in and near town. Damage to the city's electrical system alone was later estimated at $125,000.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding of several streets in and near Brookings. Several vehicles stalled on the flooded roads, and a few were floated.

Thunderstorm winds caused widespread tree damage, including numerous trees blown down. Several houses and garages were damaged by tree debris, and the winds blew shingles off roofs. The winds damaged siding and roofs. Power lines and poles were blown down, resulting in a power outage. Several streets in Elkton were blocked by trees.
Thunderstorm winds caused tree damage, including several trees blown down.
Thunderstorm winds flattened a Morton building.
Thunderstorm winds damaged a silo and a barn. The winds also caused tree damage, including several trees snapped off.
Thunderstorm winds blew down numerous power lines along U.S. Highway 14, and caused tree damage.
Thunderstorm winds blew down weather observation equipment and caused tree damage, including up to 8 inch diameter branches blown down.

A tornado destroyed a shelter belt, damaged a Morton building, and damaged several garages, one of which was moved off its foundation. The tornado also caused widespread tree damage, including several trees snapped off at the base.
Thunderstorm winds caused tree damage, including branches around 4 inches in diameter blown down. The winds were accompanied by nickel size hail.
Nickel size hail was accompanied by damaging thunderstorm winds.
Non tornadic thunderstorm winds blew down trees, power poles, and power lines, destroyed a highway shop, and blew the roof off a pallet business.

A tornado destroyed several outbuildings and storage buildings, took the roofs off several other structures, and otherwise damaged the siding and roofs of several structures including some homes. Widespread tree damage included several trees blown down and debarking at tree tops.
Thunderstorm winds blew down trees and power lines, and blew over a truck.
Thunderstorm winds destroyed a grain bin, ripped a door off the side of a house, blew over a truck, and caused widespread tree damage, including several trees blown down.
Large hail was accompanied by damaging thunderstorm wind gusts.
Thunderstorm winds caused tree damage, including a few trees uprooted. The winds were accompanied by quarter size hail.
Thunderstorm winds caused widespread tree damage, including trees greater than 2 1/2 feet in diameter blown down in Garvin Park. The winds also destroyed a barn.

Thunderstorm winds damaged several homes and at least one barn, including parts of roofs torn off and shingles blown away. The winds also caused widespread tree damage, including trees up to 2 1/2 feet in diameter snapped off. Additional damage was done to roofs and siding of homes and other structures by falling trees and tree debris.  Several grain bins were destroyed. The winds blew down power poles and lines, causing a power outage.

Thunderstorm winds caused widespread tree damage, including numerous trees blown down. Several roads were blocked by fallen trees. Roofs and siding of several homes were damaged directly by the wind, and also by falling trees and wind blown tree debris. The winds also blew down power poles and lines, causing a power outage. The winds were accompanied by large hail.
Large hail, driven by damaging winds, broke windows, dented vehicles, and caused an unknown amount of crop damage.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding of several streets in Marshall.
Large hail, in combination with heavy rain, caused damage to soybean crops.
Thunderstorm winds caused tree damage, including a few large branches blown down. The winds were accompanied by hail of unknown size with no hail damage noticed.
Thunderstorm winds and resulting waves tipped over several boats and damaged docks on both sides of Lake Madison.
Thunderstorm winds caused tree damage, including a few trees blown down.
Thunderstorm winds caused tree damage, including large branches blown down, and one old tree snapped off.
Heavy rainfall of 3 to 7 inches caused flash flooding of numerous fields and several roads.

Heavy rainfall measured at 6 inches caused flash flooding of numerous roads in and near Dell Rapids, and caused flooding of Rocky Run Creek, inundating South Dakota Highway 115 on the south end of Dell Rapids and forcing its closure.

Thunderstorm winds, accompanied by large hail, caused an unknown amount of damage to corn crops.

Thunderstorm winds caused tree and power line damage, resulting in a power outage. Up to 6 inch diameter branches were blown down.

Heavy rainfall of up to 5 inches caused flash flooding of roads and fields. Roads flooded included numerous streets in the town of Spirit Lake, and U.S. Highway 71 near Arnolds Park with 2 feet of water flowing over the highway.
Thunderstorm winds caused tree damage, including several trees blown down. The winds also damaged a garage, blew down power poles and lines, and blew down 18 gravestones at a cemetery.

Heavy rain of 5.9 inches caused flash flooding of some roads and yards.

Heavy rainfall, measured at up to 5.75 inches, caused flash flooding of many streets and yards in Sioux Falls, with several vehicles becoming stranded. The water was deep enough on some roads to make it difficult for police and rescue units to reach some stranded motorists, and a few roads became impassable. Water was also reported in basements.

Flooding from upstream spring snowmelt and subsequent heavy rain continued at major to record levels through July. Lowlands along the river including several roads and recreational areas remained flooded. The river began a very slow general fall late in the month. The highest stage at Chamberlain was a record 10.1 feet above flood stage on July 8th.

Flooding from upstream spring snowmelt and subsequent heavy rain continued at major to record levels through July. Lowlands along the river including numerous roads and recreational areas and some homes remained flooded. The river began a very slow general fall late in the month. The highest stage near Greenwood was a record 8.9 feet above flood stage on July 12th.

Flooding from upstream spring snowmelt and subsequent heavy rain, affecting mainly the east shore of the Missouri River, also continued to affect parts of the Gregory County shore. A few roads and recreation areas near the river remained flooded.

Flooding from upstream spring snowmelt and subsequent heavy rain continued at major levels through July. Lowlands along the river including numerous roads, parks, recreational areas including a golf course, and several homes remained flooded. Thousands of acres of usually dry land, including several farms, remained flooded. The river began a very slow general fall late in the month. The highest stage near Springfield was 4.6 feet above flood stage on July 12th. This was only 0.2 feet below the record crest recorded in June.

Flooding from upstream spring snowmelt and subsequent heavy rain continued at major levels through July. Lowlands along the river east of Lewis and Clark Lake including numerous roads, parks, recreational areas and several homes remained flooded. The flooding included the Larson's Landing development west of Yankton with most homes and recreational vehicles there remaining flooded. Thousands of acres of usually dry land, including several farms, remained flooded. The river began a very slow general fall late in the month. The highest stage at Yankton was 6.1 feet above flood stage on July 7th. This was equal to the highest level recorded in June.

Flooding from upstream spring snowmelt and subsequent heavy rain continued at major levels through July. Lowlands along the river including numerous roads, parks, recreational areas and several homes remained flooded. Thousands of acres of usually dry land, including several farms, remained flooded. The river began a very slow general fall late in the month. The river reached record high stages near Gayville and near Maskell, Nebraska in early July.

Flooding from upstream spring snowmelt and subsequent heavy rain continued at major levels through July. Lowlands along the river including numerous roads, parks, recreational areas and homes remained flooded. Most of the Dakota Dunes community remained flooded, with many residents and business owners still displaced. Thousands of acres of usually dry land, including several farms, remained flooded. The river began a very slow general fall late in the month. The highest stage near Ponca, Nebraska, was 8.3 feet above flood stage on July 11th. This was equal to the highest level recorded in June.

Flooding from upstream spring snowmelt and subsequent heavy rain continued at major levels through July. Lowlands along the river including numerous roads, parks, recreational areas and homes remained flooded. Thousands of acres of usually dry land, including several farms, remained flooded. The river began a very slow general fall late in the month. The highest stage near Ponca was 8.3 feet above flood stage on July 11th. This was equal to the highest level recorded in June.

Flooding from upstream spring snowmelt and subsequent heavy rain continued at major levels through July. Lowlands along the river including numerous roads, parks, recreational areas and homes remained flooded. Many residents earlier evacuated from their homes and at least 100 businesses could not return. Thousands of acres of usually dry land, including several farms, remained flooded. The river began a very slow general fall late in the month. The highest stage at South Sioux City was 5.3 feet above flood stage on July 21st. This was just above the highest level recorded in June.

Flooding from upstream spring snowmelt and subsequent heavy rain continued at major levels through July. Lowlands along the river including numerous roads, parks, recreational areas and homes remained flooded. Resident evacuated from their homes before July still could not return. The flooding included the Riverboat Museum and Welcome Center in Sioux City. Over 10 thousand acres of usually dry land, including several farms, remained flooded. The river began a very slow general fall late in the month. The highest stage at South Sioux City, Nebraska, was 5.3 feet above flood stage on July 21st. This was just above the highest level recorded in June.

Moderate to major flooding of the James River, ongoing since the snowmelt season in March, continued through July. Farmland and other lowlands near the river remained flooded, with the water level varying slightly up and down due to sporadic heavy rainfall. The highest stage at Huron was 6.3 feet above flood stage on July 27th, a little higher than the peak stage of June, but not as high as peak levels earlier in the Spring.

Moderate to major flooding of the James River, ongoing since the snowmelt season in March, continued through July. Farmland and other lowlands near the river remained flooded, with the water level varying slightly up and down due to sporadic heavy rainfall. The highest stage near Forestburg was 4.0 feet above flood stage on July 1st, slightly higher than the peak stage of June, but not as high as peak levels earlier in the Spring.

Moderate to major flooding of the James River, ongoing since the snowmelt season in March, continued through July. Farmland and other lowlands near the river remained flooded, with the water level varying slightly up and down due to sporadic heavy rainfall. The highest stage near Mitchell was 4.9 feet above flood stage on July 3rd, slightly higher than the peak stage of June, but not as high as peak levels earlier in the Spring.

Moderate to major flooding of the James River, ongoing since the snowmelt season in March, continued through July. Farmland and other lowlands near the river remained flooded, with the water level varying slightly up and down due to sporadic heavy rainfall.

Moderate to major flooding of the James River, ongoing since the snowmelt season in March, continued through July. Farmland and other lowlands near the river remained flooded, with the water level varying slightly up and down due to sporadic heavy rainfall. The highest stage northeast of Scotland was 3.3 feet above flood stage on July 7th, slightly higher than the peak stage of June, but not as high as peak levels earlier in the Spring.

Moderate to major flooding of the James River, ongoing since the snowmelt season in March, continued through July. Farmland and other lowlands near the river remained flooded, with the water level varying slightly up and down due to sporadic heavy rainfall. The highest stage near Yankton was 4.6 feet above flood stage on July 7th, almost a foot higher than the peak stage of June, but still 2.7 feet below the peak level earlier in the Spring.

Minor flooding redeveloped along the Big Sioux River, then subsided during the month. A few lowlands along the river were flooded. The highest stages were less than a foot above flood stage at Bruce and near Brookings.
Minor flooding redeveloped along the Big Sioux River, then subsided during the month. A few lowlands along the river were flooded.

Minor flooding redeveloped along the Big Sioux River, then subsided during the month. A few lowlands along the river were flooded, including some parkland in Sioux Falls. The highest stages were 1.7 feet above flood stage at Dell Rapids, and 2.0 feet above flood stage at the Sioux Falls North Cliff Avenue gage.
Minor to marginally moderate flooding redeveloped along the Big Sioux River, then subsided during the month. A few lowlands along the river were flooded, including some farmland.

Moderate to major flooding redeveloped along the Big Sioux River, then subsided during the month. Lowlands along the river were flooded, including farmland and several roads. The highest stages were 5.0 feet above flood stage at the Hawarden, Iowa gage, and 4.0 feet above flood stage at Akron, Iowa, both on July 18th.
Minor to marginally moderate flooding redeveloped along the Big Sioux River, then subsided during the month. A few lowlands along the river were flooded, including some farmland.

Moderate flooding redeveloped along the Big Sioux River, then subsided during the month. Lowlands along the river were flooded, including some farmland and a few roads. The highest stage at Hawarden was 5.0 feet above flood stage on July 18th.

Moderate to major flooding redeveloped along the Big Sioux River, then subsided during the month. Lowlands along the river were flooded, including some farmland and a few roads. The highest stage at Akron was 4.0 feet above flood stage on July 18th.

Minor flooding along the Big Sioux River near where the river joined the Missouri River resulted from backing of water from the flooded Missouri River. The flooding had only a small additional impact to the area with the Missouri River flooding being the main problem. The highest stage at Sioux City was 2.9 feet above flood stage on July 20th.

Major flooding of the Little Sioux River resulted from runoff caused by heavy rain. Considerable farmland, other lowlands, and several roads were flooded. The river crested at a record 5.5 feet above flood stage near Milford on July 15th.

Major flooding of the Little Sioux River resulted from runoff caused by heavy rain. Considerable farmland, other lowlands, and several roads were flooded. The river crested at 6.5 feet above flood stage at Spencer on July 16th.

Major flooding of the Little Sioux River resulted from runoff caused by heavy rain. Considerable farmland, other lowlands, and several roads were flooded. The river crested at 4.6 feet above flood stage at Linn Grove on July 17th.

Major flooding of the Little Sioux River resulted from runoff caused by heavy rain. Considerable farmland, other lowlands, and several roads were flooded. Roads closed due to flooding included U.S. Highway 59 near Cherokee, and Main Street in Cherokee. The river crested at 5.7 feet above flood stage at Cherokee on July 19th.

Moderate flooding of the Little Sioux River resulted from runoff caused by heavy rain. Farmland, other lowlands, and  a few roads were flooded. The river crested at 1.7 feet above flood stage at Correctionville on July 21st.

Major flooding of the Ocheyedan River resulted from runoff caused by heavy rain. Farmland, other lowlands, and  a few roads were flooded. The river crested at 3.6 feet above flood stage at near Spencer on July 15th.
Runoff from heavy rain caused continued record flooding of Platte Creek, with several roads under water. The creek crested at a record 2.7 feet above flood stage near Platte on July 8th.
Heavy rain caused minor lowland flooding of the Rock River, including some flooded parkland and farmland. The river crested at 2.5 feet above flood stage at Rock Rapids on July 16th.
Runoff from heavy rain caused minor lowland flooding along Pipestone Creek. The creek crested at 1.2 feet above flood stage at Pipestone on July 11th.
Heavy rain caused Split Rock Creek to flood, with lowlands along the creek and a few county roads affected. The creek crested at 4.2 feet above flood stage near Jasper on July 14th.
Heavy rain caused Split Rock Creek to flood, with lowlands along the creek and a few county roads affected. The creek crested at 4.2 feet above flood stage near Jasper on July 14th.

Runoff from heavy rain caused moderate flooding of Split Rock Creek, with lowlands along the creek and a few county roads affected. The creek crested at 3.0 feet above flood stage at Corson on July 15th.

Flooding from upstream spring snowmelt and subsequent heavy rain continued at major levels at the start of August, with lowlands along the river including several roads and recreational areas remaining flooded. The river fell slowly during the month, falling below flood stage at Chamberlain on August 22nd. The highest stage at Chamberlain was 5.5 feet above flood stage on August 1st.

Flooding from upstream spring snowmelt and subsequent heavy rain continued at major levels at the start of August. Lowlands along the river including numerous roads and recreational areas and some homes remaining flooded. The river fell slowly during most of the month. The highest stage near Greenwood was 8.2 feet above flood stage on August 6th.

Flooding from upstream spring snowmelt and subsequent heavy rain, affecting mainly the east shore of the Missouri River, also continued to affect parts of the Gregory County shore early in the month. A few roads and recreational areas near the river remained flooded.

Flooding from upstream spring snowmelt and subsequent heavy rain continued at moderate to major levels at the start of August. Lowlands along the river including numerous roads, parks, recreational areas including a golf course, and several homes remaining flooded. Thousands of acres of usually dry land, including several farms, remained flooded. The river fell slowly during most of the month. The highest stage near Springfield was 3.9 feet above flood stage on August 1st.

Flooding from upstream spring snowmelt and subsequent heavy rain continued at moderate to major levels at the start of August.  Lowlands along the river east of Lewis and Clark Lake including numerous roads, parks, recreational areas and several homes remained flooded. The flooding included the Larson's Landing development west of Yankton with most homes and recreational vehicles there remaining flooded. Thousands of acres of usually dry land, including several farms, remained flooded.  The river fell slowly during the month. The highest stage at Yankton was 5.5 feet above flood stage on August 1st.

Flooding from upstream spring snowmelt and subsequent heavy rain continued at  moderate levels at the start of August.  Lowlands along the river including numerous roads, parks, recreational areas and several homes remained flooded. Thousands of acres of usually dry land, including several farms, remained flooded. The river fell slowly during the month. The highest stage at Gayville was 1.4 feet above flood stage on August 1st.

Flooding from upstream spring snowmelt and subsequent heavy rain continued at  moderate to major levels at the start of August.  Lowlands along the river including numerous roads, parks, recreational areas and homes remained flooded. Thousands of acres of usually dry land, including several farms, remained flooded. Most of the Dakota Dunes community remained flooded, with many residents and business owners still displaced. The river fell slowly during the month. The highest stage near Ponca, Nebraska, was a record 8.6 feet above flood stage on August 1st.

Flooding from upstream spring snowmelt and subsequent heavy rain continued at  moderate to major levels at the start of August.  Lowlands along the river including numerous roads, parks, recreational areas and homes remained flooded. Thousands of acres of usually dry land, including several farms, remained flooded. The river fell slowly during the month. The highest stage near Ponca was a record 8.6 feet above flood stage on August 1st.

Flooding from upstream spring snowmelt and subsequent heavy rain continued at  moderate to major levels at the start of August.  Lowlands along the river including numerous roads, parks, recreational areas and homes remained flooded. Many residents earlier evacuated from their homes and at least 100 businesses could not return before late in the month. Thousands of acres of usually dry land, including several farms, remained flooded. The river fell slowly during the month. The highest stage at South Sioux City was 4.3 feet above flood stage on August 1st. The river there fell below flood stage on August 25th.

Flooding from upstream spring snowmelt and subsequent heavy rain continued at  moderate levels at the start of August.  Lowlands along the river including numerous roads, parks, recreational areas and homes remained flooded. Many residents earlier evacuated from their homes and at least 100 businesses could not return before late in the month. The flooding included the Riverboat Museum and Welcome Center in Sioux City. Over 10 thousand acres of usually dry land, including several farms, remained flooded. The river fell slowly during the month. The highest stage at South Sioux City, Nebraska, was 4.3 feet above flood stage on August 1st, with the river there falling below flood stage on August 25th.

Minor flooding of the Big Sioux River, caused by backing of Missouri River floodwaters, continued at the start of August before ending by August 10th. The flooding in the North Sioux City and Dakota Dunes area had little additional impact to the Missouri River flooding.

Minor flooding along the Big Sioux River near where the river joined the Missouri River continued at the start of August as a result of backing of water from the flooded Missouri River. The flooding had little additional impact to the Missouri River flooding in the area. The highest stage at Sioux City was 1 foot above flood stage on August 1st, with the river falling below flood stage on August 10th.

Thunderstorm winds caused widespread damage in the south part of Flandreau. Roofs on homes, apartment buildings, and other buildings were blown off or damaged. The roof of a large church was blown off, and parts of the roof damaged nearby homes. The Flandreau city office building had part of its south wall blown off, resulting in interior damage to ceiling tiles and insulation. Siding on other walls of this building and on numerous homes was damaged. Tree damage was widespread, including several trees blown down or uprooted. The winds blew down power lines, leaving parts of the city without power for almost three hours.

Heavy rainfall of up to 6 inches caused flash flooding of numerous roads, parks, fields, other low areas, and buildings including homes. At least 90 homes were heavily damaged in Madison by the flooding, including at least two with basement walls washed out. A basement wall of a dentists business was also washed out and the basement flooded with 9 feet of water. Numerous personal possessions in flooded homes and businesses were destroyed. The flash flooding included Memorial Creek, and there was a fatality when an out of state visitor drowned when attempting to cross the flooded creek. While this fatality and most of the damage was in Madison, many rural roads and fields were flooded in the area, and east to near the town of Wentworth.

Much below normal rainfall continued to aggravate existing long term dry soil conditions, and also resulted in a lack of even short term relief. This increased stress on crops with the stress becoming increasingly visible. Damage in the form of reduced yields became certain, but the amount of yield reduction was still highly unknown because of the long time remaining before harvest, and the unknown future weather during that time. At the end of the month, corn crops were judged to be the most susceptible to the reduced yields, due to the lack of moisture during the tasseling period, while soybeans had more recovery potential if significant rain were to fall in the near future.

The future effect of the lack of soil moisture on next spring and summer's farming was feared if the dryness were to continue. Otherwise, few new effects of the drought were noted during the month due to the seasonally low water usage and need.

A tornado crossed the Missouri River from Dakota County in Nebraska and entered Union County. The tornado severely damaged the roof of a house, and collapsed a chimney, carport and porch roof, and the walls of a garage in the same house. The tornado also caused tree damage, including trunks snapped, overturned an irrigation system, and  damaged the roof, siding, and/or gutters of at least four other houses.

A tornado severely damaged the roof and gutters of a house, and the walls and roof of at least two storage equipment buildings. The tornado caused tree damage, including trunks snapped and large branches blown down, damaged a road sign, blew down or crushed several grain bins, blew down power poles and lines, and flattened corn crops. One of the destroyed grain bins was wrapped around a house, causing damage to the roof, siding, and gutters of the house. The tornado then crossed the Big Sioux River into Plymouth County Iowa.
A tornado developed in northern Dakota County and caused no reported damage before crossing the Missouri River into Union County of South Dakota.
A tornado crossed the Big Sioux River into Plymouth County from Union County in South Dakota. The tornado caused no reported damage in Plymouth County before dissipating.

A tornado severely damaged or destroyed about 10 houses, collapsing most walls on a few of the houses, tearing most of the roofs off other houses, and shifting what was left of some houses off their foundations. The tornado caused significant damage to roofs, windows, and siding of additional houses. Numerous farm outbuildings, storage buildings, and a few silos were destroyed or severely damaged. The tornado also destroyed or damaged several pieces of farm equipment, caused significant tree damage, including numerous trunks snapped or uprooted and other trees stripped, and blew down power poles and lines. The tornado then crossed into Cherokee County.
A tornado, crossing into Chrerokee County from Woodbury County, damaged power poles, power lines, and trees.

A tornado, crossing into Dixon County from Wayne County, severely damaged the roofs of two houses, one of which was a manufactured house, and caused damage to the siding and windows of the houses. Windows of at least one other house were blown out. The tornado also overturned a camper, destroyed or severely damaged a grain bin, numerous farm outbuildings, farm storage buildings, several pieces of farm equipment, and flattened corn crops in several areas. The tornado caused tree damage along its path, including trees uprooted and snapped off at the trunks, and blew down power poles and power lines.

A tornado, crossing into Woodbury County from Monona County Iowa, severely damaged at least two houses, collapsing two walls and blowing the roof off one of the houses. The tornado also destroyed or damaged numerous farm outbuildings and storage buildings, including several structures at a hog farm, and a large metal storage building. The tornado also destroyed open air buildings at a dairy farm. The tornado blew down power lines and poles, and caused considerable tree damage, including trees snapped off at their trunks. Corn crops were flattened in a few areas.

The tornado also tore the roof off a farm storage building, tore the metal roof off a metal building, blew down electrical poles, and caused tree damage, including several trees snapped off at the trunks.
